analysis.one_liner: Makes it much harder to certify consumer class actions and forces public disclosure of asbestos trust claims.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 211-188 on a near party-line vote on January 8, 2016, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar federal courts from approving a class action for money damages unless plaintiffs prove that every single class member suffered an injury of the same type and scope as the named plaintiffs. Very few large class actions — over a faulty drug, a data breach, a defective product — involve injuries identical in degree, so this standard would end most class litigation in federal court. The bill also requires asbestos bankruptcy trusts to publish quarterly reports naming claimants and their exposure histories, and to share that information with companies being sued over asbestos.
analysis.who_benefits: Large corporate defendants — drug makers, banks, insurers, automakers, and other product companies — that face consumer class actions. The uniform-injury requirement would make it nearly impossible to certify the broad classes that generate the biggest aggregate recoveries, so companies would mostly face individual suits instead, many of which are never brought because the stakes for one person are too small. Asbestos defendants also gain a new tool: quarterly public disclosures of every trust claim, which they can use to cross-check and challenge claimants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large corporate defendants facing class-action liability

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits federal courts from certifying any class action seeking money for personal injury or economic loss unless plaintiffs affirmatively show that each class member suffered the same type and scope of injury as the named representatives.

Because injuries in most large class actions vary in degree — people react differently to the same drug or product defect — the uniform-injury standard would eliminate certification of most such classes, replacing many-person aggregate suits with individual claims that are often too small to file.

Asbestos bankruptcy trusts would have to file quarterly public reports describing each claim and its basis, and on request provide claim information to any party litigating asbestos liability, giving defendants material to dispute payouts.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and injured people, who would lose the class-action device that lets many people with small-dollar harms from one company's conduct join together in one case when no single claim justifies a lawsuit. Asbestos claimants would also bear privacy costs, since their names, exposure histories, and claim details would go on the public court record.

drawbacks.text: The same-type-and-scope requirement applies even where everyone was harmed by the same conduct but to different degrees — the typical fact pattern in defective-drug and product cases — so the bill's remedy for overbroad suits is to eliminate the class device in most meritorious cases too.

Quarterly public reports naming claimants, their exposure histories, and the basis for payments would put injured people's private medical and exposure details on the public docket, and the information must also be handed to companies defending asbestos suits.
The reporting and disclosure requirements apply to trusts already operating from bankruptcies completed before the bill, forcing compliance on cases that were resolved decades ago.

Supporters' good-faith case is that some class actions settle for big lawyer fees and small class payouts, and that some asbestos trusts have paid questionable claims; the uniform-injury rule and the transparency provision are blunt responses that reach valid claims along with abusive ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The asbestos transparency provision has a defensible core — checking trust payments against defendants' records to catch duplicate or inflated claims — though its cost to claimant privacy is real. The class-action provision is the opposite of a targeted fix: it does not police fee arrangements or coupon settlements; it simply bars certification of any class whose members' injuries differ in extent, which covers most genuine mass-harm cases. Consumers with small-dollar injuries would lose their only practical remedy, while the savings flow to the companies that caused the harm. The costs outweigh the benefits for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a party-line vote, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never brought it up, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 22, 2015 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The committee ordered it reported amended on a 15-10 vote in June 2015 and formally reported it on November 5, 2015.

During House floor consideration on January 8, 2016, a series of Democratic amendments — from Reps. Cohen, Conyers, Deutch, Moore, Waters, Johnson, Jackson Lee, and Nadler — all failed; each would have narrowed the bill or created exemptions.
A motion to recommit with instructions to exempt schoolchildren exposed to asbestos from the trust-disclosure provision failed 173-227, with 172 of 188 Democrats voting yes and only 1 Republican.
The House passed the bill 211-188 with 1 member voting present: 211 of 245 Republicans voted yes and 16 voted no, while 172 of 188 Democrats voted no and none voted yes.
The Senate received the bill on January 11, 2016 and referred it to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never reported it or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and asbestos claimants kept the class-action tool and their private claim records, and corporate defendants continue to face broad class litigation as they did before. Had the bill become law, the gain would have gone to companies facing class actions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers who kept the class-action remedy

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 211 of 245 Republicans voted yes and 16 no, while 172 of 188 Democrats voted no and none voted yes; the same split appeared on the motion to recommit (172 of 188 Democrats yes, 1 Republican).

industries.industry: Corporate defendants in consumer litigation (drug makers, banks, insurers, automakers, product manufacturers)
industries.note: The uniform-injury standard would eliminate certification of most broad class actions, shielding these companies from aggregate liability for products and practices that harm many people in varying degrees. Their gain is the loss of consumers' main remedy for small-dollar harms.

Quarterly public trust reports and mandatory disclosure to litigation parties would give these companies material to challenge and reduce trust payouts. The transparency aim targets real duplicate and inflated claims, but its cost falls on claimants' privacy and on valid claims.

The certification bar would eliminate most large class litigation, the practice area where plaintiffs' lawyers aggregate small claims. When class actions shrink, the people those suits compensate shrink with them.

Trusts would bear quarterly reporting costs and must hand claim information to defendants on request, including for trusts formed before the bill. Their function — paying legitimate claimants — becomes harder to administer.
